title: Jewish music
hookLine: klezmer, Sephardi songs, cantorial chant and new music

cards: Late on a Friday night, the plates are cleared and the candles are low. Nobody says anything. Then someone at the end of the table starts humming.
No words, just a line of sound: yai dai dai, rising and falling. Somebody joins the second time through, then a few more. A child taps the beat on the table.
By the fourth time, the whole table is singing a tune with no words at all, and somehow everyone knows what it means.

teach.b: Music is there from the start of the story. At the sea, after the crossing, Miriam takes a timbrel in her hand and the women follow her, dancing and singing.
When King Saul is tormented, young David plays the harp, and the spirit troubling Saul leaves him. And the Psalms keep asking for more: "O sing unto the LORD a new song." A new one.
The psalm isn't content with the old tunes. In the synagogue, even reading is music.
The Torah is chanted aloud, following small marks written above and below the words, and the cantor, the hazzan, leads the prayers in chant.
Some cantors became well-known for it, carrying a whole congregation on one held note. Then the music traveled with the people.
In Eastern Europe, Yiddish-speaking musicians called klezmorim played at weddings, with clarinet and fiddle that seem to laugh and weep in the same phrase.
Sephardi families, carried far from Spain, kept singing in Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish language: lullabies, love songs, wedding songs, often passed mother to daughter.
Mizrahi singers carried the scales of Baghdad, Cairo and Sanaa.

teach.h: THE NIGGUN, AND A NEW SONG.
teach.b: Hasidic communities treasure the niggun, the wordless tune from the Friday night table; some Hasidic teachers said a melody can climb where words can't follow.

And the music keeps arriving: choirs, rock bands, new settings of old prayers, the new song the psalm keeps asking for. Different instruments, different languages, different scales, and the music holds all of it.

how: Jews sing at the Shabbat table, hear the Torah chanted and the prayers led by a cantor in synagogue, dance to klezmer and other music at weddings, and keep Ladino, Mizrahi, Hasidic and new Jewish songs alive at home and in concert.

games.q: you're young David, called to the court of King Saul, who is tormented and can't find rest. what do you bring?
o: a harp, to play for him.
a scroll, to read to him.
games.why: David plays the harp, and the spirit troubling Saul leaves him. the story trusts music to reach where words don't.

practice: Listen first to what's already around you: the hum of a fridge, traffic, your own breath, rising and falling like a tune.
Then, if you like, hum something low with no words, the way the Friday night table does, and notice where it sits in your chest. If you pray, you can let the music carry your prayer without words.

wordCard.voice: Jewish music. Miriam's timbrel, the chanted Torah, klezmer, Ladino songs, Mizrahi scales, the wordless niggun, and the new song still being written. Today's word.
